item.title: Comment on Net neutrality, we hardly knew ye by MS
item.description:
When the FCC under the first Trump administration tore up the Open Internet Order and washed its hands of the net neutrality issue, major states like California and New York stepped up with their own state laws addressing the issue. ISPs have so far concluded that it's not worth deviating from the behaviors mandated by the Open Internet Order if they can't do it everywhere. So if you believe that today's Internet is a success, it is a success achieved while largely adhering to Open Internet principles, something that is likely to continue notwithstanding the recent Sixth Circuit ruling.

item.title: Comment on Net neutrality, we hardly knew ye by andrew97
item.description:
I think this misremembers what the net neutrality fight was about. The concern was not that bandwidth was scarce, it was that the backbones were controlled by a few big providers who could throttle bandwidth of competitors, or bid up access fees to favour incumbents. The argument was that keeping the playing field level would promote disruptive innovation. And indeed, the USA ended up with an extremely vibrant startup ecosystem. Would this have happened without net neutrality, when the telcos could kill any service they didn't like? I don't know but I think it's weird to dismiss the idea.

item.title: Comment on Thursday assorted links by Alabamian
item.description:
1. I admittedly didn't get into the weeds of this, but the theory here seems pretty strange.

The authors note that self-reports of a "bisexual" sexual orientation have markedly increased over time, especially among women, and that: "[T]he vast majority of bisexual men and women who do have a cohabiting partner are actually in a relationship with a person of the opposite gender. . . . in the 2013-2018 period, about 90% of all partnered bisexual men and women in the U.S. were in a different-sex relationship."

Instead of taking that as evidence of: (i) preference falsification in reporting of sexual identity; or, more benignly (ii) a shifting conception of what it means to be "bisexual"; the authors take this as evidence that many more of these "bisexual" people yearn to be cohabitating with a same-sex sexual partner but aren't because of a "same-sex penalty" which the authors set out to characterize.

That all seems quite wrong-headed to me.

item.title: Comment on Tax incidence theory and congestion tolls by Matt
item.description:
Despite what Cowen was saying a few days ago, it looks like travel times into lower Manhattan have already decreased quite a bit, and no doubt it's easier to find parking, too. This may well encourage some people to come, who are coming for the specific reason of going to a restaurant! The posts on this topic are very strange, and show a weird desperation. Travel into Manhattan is a scarce and desirable thing - why does Cowen think it should be priced at zero?
